extracted.intended_audience: regulatory practitioners, agency staff, administrative lawyers, and public commenters involved in federal rulemaking and notice-and-comment proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Glossary-style compilation of federal administrative law terms that set out procedural requirements, substantive standards, and best practices for conducting, participating in, and reviewing federal rulemaking (especially notice-and-comment rulemaking). Useful for agencies, counsel, and public commenters preparing or evaluating rules and rulemaking records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) minimum procedural steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The law spells out the minimum steps that an agency must follow when it issues most rules — publish a proposal in the Federal Register, invite and consider comment, and issue a final rule at least 30 days before its effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may also be required to follow additional procedural requirements in other statutes or agency rules; additional rules announced by an agency are binding if the agency has announced it will follow them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal rulemaking (Section 553 notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal rulemaking involves: (1) publishing a proposed rule in the Federal Register; (2) inviting public comment; (3) considering the public comment; and (4) publishing a final rule in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency has discretion whether to hold hearings; any 'interested person' may submit comments. Informal rulemaking must produce a record showing the agency took a 'hard look' at evidence and alternatives because courts will review it thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking Exceptions (including good cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of rules are excepted from notice-and-comment (e.g., military/foreign affairs, agency management/personnel, public property, loans, grants, benefits, contracts) and other broad exceptions include interpretive rules, general statements of policy, and rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 553(b)(B) 'good cause' exception permits dispensing with notice and comment when procedures are 'impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest' — but courts construe these narrowly and agencies must give supporting reasons. Section 553(d)(3) allows making a rule effective immediately upon finding good cause, avoiding the 30-day delayed effective date (also construed narrowly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An ANPRM is used to obtain public participation in the formulation of a regulatory change typically before the agency has done significant research; it may be called a 'notice of inquiry' or 'request for comments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA does not require ANPRMs and an agency cannot use an ANPRM’s notice-and-comment period as the only basis for issuing a final rule — the agency still must issue an NPRM before issuing a final rule on that subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency makes significant substantive changes between the NPRM and the final rule, the public must be given an opportunity to comment on the revisions, typically by issuing an SNPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Significant substantive changes’ mean new requirements beyond the scope of the NPRM. Agency may proceed on unaffected parts while SNPRM comments are pending. This practice follows court decisions and the Logical Outgrowth Test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct final rule procedure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct final rule is published first as a final rule with a statement indicating the rule will take effect in X days unless someone submits a significant adverse or negative comment (or a notice of intent to do so) within a stated number of days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an adverse comment is received and the agency wishes to proceed, the agency must republish the document as a proposed rule and proceed with normal notice-and-comment rulemaking. Direct final rulemaking is intended for non-controversial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim final rule / 'final rule with request for comments' practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An interim final rule is a device where agencies publish a final rule and invite post-promulgation comment, typically relying on a 'good cause' justification to skip prior NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'final rule with request for comments' is more accurate than 'interim final rule' because many such rules lack a termination date; original FAA practice coined the device. Use of this technique requires a justifiable 'good cause' showing; courts scrutinize such findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docket and use of docket number
rubrics_metrics.description: A docket is the file opened for a rulemaking or adjudicatory action and usually includes all relevant public information that the agency intends to use in reaching a decision (e.g., public comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing to an agency about a proceeding, it is important to use the appropriate docket number so submissions reach the correct destination. Agencies have varying docket identification systems; many dockets are now electronic via Regulations.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking record / required contents for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: A rulemaking record for informal rulemaking normally contains the NPRM, any studies or reports referred to in the NPRM, public comments, records of hearings or meetings, and the final rule document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must anticipate judicial review and include in the administrative record anything they will use to support policy decisions; the record should show the agency took a hard look at relevant evidence and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analytical requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: RFA requires agencies to consider the effects of any proposed rule on 'small entities' and, if the rule will affect a significant number of small entities, prepare a Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (RFA) at both proposed and final stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis must include: (1) estimate of the number and type of small entities to be affected; (2) detailed description of recordkeeping and compliance requirements; and (3) discussion of alternatives to reduce burdens. SBREFA added judicial review and obligations to provide assistance and modify enforcement for small businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: UMRA Title II requires agencies (excluding independent regulatory agencies) to prepare a written assessment of effects of any proposed or final rule that contains a Federal mandate likely to result in expenditures of $100 million or more (adjusted annually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 204(a) requires a process to permit timely input by elected state/local/tribal officers on significant intergovernmental mandates. While UMRA is enforced in Presidential Review of Rules, judicial review is quite limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact statements and required analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes and Executive Orders require agencies to perform impact analyses and publish 'impact statements'—e.g., environmental impact statements (NEPA), Regulatory Flexibility Analyses, Unfunded Mandates assessments, and Paperwork Reduction Act analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Orders (e.g., E.O. 12866, E.O. 13563) require assessments of costs and benefits for major rules and other specific analyses (federalism, takings, energy, children’s health, tribal impacts). OIRA guidance (e.g., Regulatory Impact Analysis Primer and OMB Circular A‑4) helps agencies prepare analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost-benefit (benefit-cost) analysis has become important in rulemaking via Presidential executive orders requiring regulatory impact analyses for major rules with significant economic impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBA forms a main basis for OIRA review. Agencies should follow OMB guidance (Circular A‑4) and E.O. requirements (historically E.O. 12291, 12866, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection Request (ICR) / Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: An ICR is the set of documents an agency submits to OMB/OIRA to obtain approval for a 'collection of information' under the Paperwork Reduction Act. Each request must be approved by OMB before the collection begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICR must provide a justification and estimate cost/time for the public to respond. Agencies submit ICRs through ROCIS. Independent regulatory agencies can override an OIRA veto by majority vote (rarely exercised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference (IBR) approval process
rubrics_metrics.description: IBR is a technique to include materials published elsewhere (e.g., industry standards) in regulations without republishing them in full text; agencies must obtain approval of the Director of the Office of the Federal Register pursuant to the APA (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations governing IBR approval are set out in Part 51 of Title 1 CFR; OFR updated IBR regulations and issued an IBR Handbook (2016). Copyrighted standards raise special issues; ACUS provided recommendations (2011-5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance documents and 'good guidance practices'
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance refers to interpretive rules, policy statements, and other materials issued to explain statutes or regulations; agencies typically state guidance is not intended to be binding but guidance often has significant practical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance does not require notice-and-comment, making it easier to issue than regulations. ACUS recommendations and OMB’s 'Good Guidance Practices' Bulletin provide best practices. Agencies should be aware that field staff often treat guidance as mandatory in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte communications rule distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte communications—off-the-record contact with decisionmakers—are improper in contested adjudications and prohibited there, but historically the APA’s bar does not apply to rulemaking (a quasi-legislative process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are free to establish stronger limits on ex parte communications in rulemaking; many limit such contacts after the NPRM and require documentation and placement in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Register publication requirements and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Register is the official daily publication for rules, proposed rules, and notices, organized into sections: 'Presidential Documents,' 'Rules and Regulations,' 'Proposed Rules,' and 'Notices'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules must include text to be codified in the CFR and a preamble with background and explanatory material. Agencies should use the Federal Register to announce meetings, petitions, availability of reports, and other notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) revision practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFR contains codified agency regulations divided into 50 titles; each title is revised annually to insert additions/amendments that appeared in the Federal Register during the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An up-to-date e-CFR is available online for current regulatory text; agencies must ensure final rule language is formatted and submitted correctly for CFR codification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act (Congressional review of rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must submit each 'rule' to both Houses of Congress and to GAO before it can take effect; a 'major' rule's effective date is automatically stayed for 60 days while Congress reviews it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress can pass a resolution of disapproval to nullify a rule; several administrations have seen use of this procedure. The process requires Congressional and Presidential approval (or veto override).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-or-capricious standard for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 706(2)(A) directs courts to invalidate agency actions found to be 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law'; applied often to review of factual basis for rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts overturn rules where policy judgments, reasoning, or factual premises are so unreasonable as to be arbitrary. For decisions after formal hearings, the 'substantial evidence' standard applies; courts treat the tests as having limited practical difference in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference doctrines (Chevron, Auer, Skidmore, Loper Bright implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron established a two-step test for judicial deference to agency statutory interpretations; Auer concerned deference to agency interpretations of their own regulations; Skidmore endorsed deference based on persuasiveness. Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron, requiring Skidmore-style persuasiveness review for statutory ambiguities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auer has been narrowed by cases and Kisor imposed guardrails; courts may treat interpretations made without notice-and-comment with lesser deference. Agencies should be cautious when relying on non-binding statements expecting Chevron-level deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking (on-the-record hearing) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking is required when statute directs that a rule may issue only after an opportunity for a 'hearing on the record' conducted under APA §§ 556-557; such proceedings are trial-like and cumbersome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of burden, few statutes require formal rulemaking; where required, agencies must follow formal hearing procedures, including record creation suitable for substantial-evidence review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid rulemaking procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid rulemaking occurs when Congress demands procedural requirements more formal than APA informal procedures but less than full formal rulemaking (e.g., creation of formal record, oral hearings, multi-stage rulemaking, detailed findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant statutes (Clean Air Act, OSHA, FTC rulemaking statute) require hybrid procedures; agencies must follow the specific statutory process in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Agenda / Unified Agenda content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unified Agenda must include, at minimum, a regulation identification number (RIN), a brief summary of the action, the legal authority for the action, any legal deadline, and the name and telephone number of a knowledgeable agency official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires listing proposed rules likely to have significant impacts on small entities and publication of regulatory flexibility agendas; publication allows public involvement before an NPRM is issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective Regulatory Review expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: E.O. 13563 requires agencies to periodically review significant regulations to identify rules that may be outmoded, ineffective, insufficient, or excessively burdensome and to modify, streamline, expand, or repeal them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.O. 13610 further specified reporting processes and deadlines for retrospective reviews; agencies must submit draft reports to OIRA twice yearly under E.O. 13610 and E.O. 12866 provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations.gov / e-rulemaking centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov serves as the central place for the public to comment on pending proposed rules, review others' comments, and access rulemaking dockets; e-rulemaking has enabled wider public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-rulemaking program moved to GSA in 2019 with governance structures (Executive Committee, Advisory Board) and workgroups; agencies and commenters should use Regulations.gov and related e-docket tools to ensure submissions are in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) response obligations and exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: FOIA requires agencies to make certain information available to the public unless it falls into one of nine exemptions (e.g., classified documents; personnel rules; statutory exemptions; trade secrets; inter-/intra-agency memoranda; personal privacy; law enforcement investigatory records; financial institution information; geological information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After receiving a FOIA request, agency has 20 working days (subject to one extension) to comply or send a written denial invoking exemptions and appeal instructions; agencies must release non-exempt portions where feasible and may charge fees subject to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism considerations and Executive Order 13132
rubrics_metrics.description: Federalism concerns require consultation with state/local/tribal governments and specify that Federal regulations may preempt state/local law only when Congress expressly authorizes it or grants clear authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.O. 13132 requires agencies to provide a 'federalism summary impact statement' and consult with state/local officials for rules with federalism implications. OMB can enforce E.O. 13132 by rejecting regulations lacking consultation or the summary statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: FACA (Federal Advisory Committee Act) requirements for outside advice
rubrics_metrics.description: FACA establishes procedures an agency must follow when seeking advice from outside groups, including chartering requirements, committee membership rules, and public participation at open meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FACA aims to ensure objectivity and public accessibility; GSA has oversight and implementing regulations (41 CFR Chapter 102-3). Agencies must consider FACA when planning consultations before or during rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) appointment and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: ALJs are appointed under the APA to preside over formal APA hearings; the APA guarantees protections (e.g., not supervised by investigators/prosecutors, exempt from performance ratings, pay set by statute, disciplined only for good cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ALJs make initial or recommended decisions subject to appeal to agency head; ALJs differ from non-ALJ hearing officers used in non-APA proceedings.
